title: Report into Serpentine Jarrahdale council details dysfunction
text:
Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale council's stated goal was improving conduct and leadership when it requested an independent monitor in April.

It was hoped the monitor's time working with the outer-suburban Perth council would improve elected member conduct and relationships with staff; however, the final report to WA local government inspector Tony Brown has detailed turmoil and dysfunction.

In her report, obtained by the ABC, monitor Dominique Mecoy alleges disrespectful behaviour.

"During the monitoring assignment, the monitor observed the alleged conduct of some council members towards other council members and staff may be contributing to psychosocial safety risks," the report states.

The report also pointed out that staff described a culture of "fear of reprisal or unfair criticism from some council members".

The monitor estimated the cost in legal fees and lost staff time of dealing with some allegations of "poor council member behaviour" to be more than $200,000 last financial year.

The shire's councillors are (from left) Joel Chan, Nathan Bishop, Reece Jerrett, Rob Coales, Courtney Mazzini, Matthew Scott and Kim Glisenti. (Facebook: Shire of Serpentine Jarrahdale)

The report outlines a 16-point action plan for the council to improve, involving training for councillors, but also notes that relationships have significantly deteriorated.

"Given the nature of some internal relationships, the monitor considered that team building may not be appropriate in an environment such as this, and more time would be required to address some of the key issues and rebuild trust," Ms Mecoy wrote.

Local government inspector Tony Brown, Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley and the Shire of Serpentine-Jarrahdale have been contacted for comment.

The council is scheduled to meet tonight for an ordinary council meeting.

Psychosocial safety a matter of law

Tash Broomhall, who runs workplace mental health consultancy Blooming Minds, if the allegations in the report are true, it could indicate that the council was in breach of workplace health and safety regulations.

"Under work health and safety regulations here in WA, it's been specifically identified that workplaces have an obligation to keep their workers safe from what are called psychosocial hazards," Dr Broomhall told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"If you've got a report where the finding is that these are not being addressed, then you could assume that that organisation is in breach of its work health and safety regulations."

Dr Broomhall said feeling psychologically unsafe at work made it very hard for workers to do their jobs effectively and for an organisation to function.

"If you don't feel safe to speak up, to challenge ideas, to be able to have issues addressed, how on earth are you then putting your full mind to the technical elements of your job? How are you able to think clearly, make decisions clearly?"

She said to address psychosocial safety concerns effectively, organisations needed to look at how problems arose, as well as tackling problematic behaviours.

"They need to look at what were the conditions in the workplace that allowed these issues to materialise in the first place," she said.

"Organisations' responsibility is not just to respond, it's to look at prevention."

title: Mother of five children killed in house fire tells inquest 'fire was everywhere'
text:
A mother whose five sons and partner died in a house fire has begun giving evidence at an inquest into their deaths.

In August 2023, 34-year-old Wayne Godinet Jr and 11-year-old Zackary, 10-year-old Harrison, four-year-old twins Kyza and Koah, and three-year-old Nickolas died of smoke inhalation after their Russell Island home burnt down.

The children's mother, Samantha Stephenson and another family member escaped the blaze unharmed.

Ms Stephenson was the first witness to give evidence at the coronial inquest, which began in Brisbane on Monday.

'There was fire everywhere'

The inquest heard on the night before the fire, Ms Stephenson and Mr Godinet Jr, who had been in an on-again, off-again relationship, had smoked marijuana together in a "chill-out zone" they had created together under the raised Queenslander home she was renting.

She said she went to sleep on one of the couches while they were cuddling between 7:30pm and 8pm after putting the three youngest boys to bed. The older boys generally went to bed later.

Ms Stephenson told the inquest the only source of light had been a lava lamp and no heaters had been turned on.

She was also asked about the location of candles and lighters in the home as well as batteries and petrol.

The charred remains of the Russell Island home after the fatal fire. (ABC News: George Roberts)

The inquest heard the only lighter in the home had been with her, and the candles had been moved downstairs after an incident a few days before the fire when one of the boys had run into his room with a lit candle.

Other tools and fuel sources were being stored under the house, the inquest heard.

Ms Stephenson told the inquest she awoke early in the morning to the feeling of Mr Godinet Jr moving or jumping onto or off the couch and heard him screaming "no", before he ran up the stairs.

She said when she tried to follow him upstairs the fire "just exploded, literally" and so instead she went outside to try and go upstairs and get her children via the external stairs.

Ms Stephenson was questioned by counsel assisting about where she had been able to see the fire when she woke up but said repeatedly fire had been "everywhere".

After going outside, she had seen her other relative on the verandah who was screaming for help. Ms Stephenson said she had told them to jump to safety.

Neighbours then called emergency services.

Eleven-year-old Zack, ten-year-old Harry, four-year-old twins, their three-year-old brother, and father Wayne Godinet died in a house fire on Russell Island. (Supplied)

'Did you start the fire?'

Counsel assisting the coroner Corinne Leach told the inquest a fire investigation had been unable to determine what sparked the deadly blaze and had been unable to rule out it "deliberate human ignition".

Ms Stephenson was asked whether she lit the fire, to which she replied she did not.

She was also asked about evidence given to police where neighbours who she lived near after the fire alleged she had made comments including that she was a "murderer" and had let "smoke kill my kids". Ms Stephenson denied having made those comments.

A member of the public, who was sitting in the gallery, became loudly upset and interjected proceedings. They were given a warning by Deputy State Corner Donald Mackenzie.

The Russell Island house burnt down in August 2023. (ABC News)

'You'll have to dumb it down for me'

The lack of compliant smoke alarms installed in the home is also forming part of the inquest.

In the months after the blaze, the home owner pleaded guilty to breaching the Fire Services Act and was fined.

Under cross-examination by the property owner's barrister Tony Kimmins, Ms Stephenson was asked about working smoke alarms in the property.

She initially told the inquest she could not recall whether there had been working smoke alarms, but later agreed she had been shown smoke alarms in a drawer in the house by the property owner.

Asked whether she did anything to organise them to be installed, Ms Stephenson became upset, asking Mr Kimmins "what would you have done" and "is this as much as you got?"

She was warned her answers were becoming "disrespectful" to counsel and to the court.

Mr Kimmins said he would "dumb it down" for her, to which she responded: "yes, you'll have to dumb it down for me".

She was asked about several inconsistencies between the initial statement she provided police and the evidence she gave in court on Monday. Ms Stephenson said she had not read her initial statement until this morning when she signed it, as when she had previously been provided with a copy of it, she had not been in the "mind" to do so.

"I've been coming out of a really bad state of denial that's lasted quite a long time," she told the inquest.

She said her memories had not changed, but some details were now clearer.

Domestic violence canvassed

Ms Stephenson agreed her relationship with Mr Godinet Jr had been "rocky" and the inquest heard he had previously been jailed for assaulting her.

She told the inquest she had wanted to sleep downstairs on the night of the fire to ensure Mr Godinet Jr did not leave with the children.

During cross-examination, Ms Stephenson agreed the pair had quickly come to the attention of police after they moved to Russell Island, and they had been called on several occasions, including to the home.

She was also played a video which the court heard showed an interaction between one of her neighbours who had called the police after hearing a heated argument between them and heard Ms Stephenson calling for help.

The inquest also saw a second video where the same neighbour tells police he heard glass breaking and heard loud arguing between the pair during an argument on the morning of the fire. Ms Stephenson said she could not recall broken glass or fighting on that day.

Claims of domestic violence, non-compliant smoke alarms and point of origin will all be canvassed during the inquest.

title: Four of our favourite potato recipes
text:
There are few staple foods as versatile or satisfying as the humble spud and if you're looking for some new twists on some classic recipes, we have you covered.

From golden-roasted rosemary and garlic spuds and a vegetarian tray bake to a bright and punchy potato salad and a vegan gratin, we have something to suit all tastes.

These garlic and rosemary-infused roast potatoes are the perfect side dish. (ABC TV: Wesley Mitton)

Alice Zaslavsky whipped up this batch of golden roasted potatoes for Zan Rowe on season two of A Bite to Eat With Alice as a tribute to Dolly Parton, who Zan had been trying to book for her show Take 5.

Sadly, Dolly has now left us, but you can still enjoy these delicious rosemary and garlic-infused roast spuds

They're crispy on the outside, tender on the inside, and certain to be a welcome addition at any dinner table.

This easy and nutritious vegetarian dinner needs little attention once it's in the oven. (ABC News: Heidi Sze)

Tray bakes are a simple and nutritious midweek meal. In addition to being easy to assemble, they require little attention once they're in the oven.

Heidi Sze's vegetarian tray bake with salt and vinegar potatoes, haloumi and greens can be tweaked to your liking with additional shallots, cheese or vinegar to suit your tastes.

This classic, creamy salad will be a welcome addition to any summer spread. (ABC News: Clementine Day)

Potato salad is a classic side at any festive event or barbecue. It can be made ahead of time, keeps well in the fridge and fills you up.

Clementine Day's rendition is punchy and super quick to pull together — about 30 minutes from start to finish — which makes it a great option for busy weeknights.

Tarragon and chives feature heavily, along with caramelised shallots and zingy pickled onion, and it's vegetarian and gluten free.

This gratin can be prepped a day ahead and then finished in the oven prior to serving, to give it a crisp, golden top. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

This rich yet light potato gratin recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon will change the way you think about the possibilities of creamy vegetable bakes.

The “cream” is made from a blend of pureed cashews and garlic, with thyme adding herbal brightness and miso paste delivering a hint of sweet-savoury depth.

This potato gratin can be eaten alone, with other roasted veggies, or with a green salad. It goes well as part of a feasting table too.

title: Coles investigates cyber attack but provides little detail
text:
Supermarket group Coles is investigating a cybersecurity incident, but has provided little detail on what occurred.

Coles disclosed the cyber attack in a statement to the stock exchange on Monday morning, saying it is currently not aware of any data being accessed or stolen as a result of the incident.

"Based on the findings of our investigation to date, we have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles' systems," the statement read.

On its website, Coles Group listed gift cards as working as normal, "no indication" of an impact on Flybuys accounts and no issues identified with Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery or QuiteLike subscriptions.

However, the retailer said it was looking into a small number of customers experiencing issues with Liquorland click-and-collect, which it was investigating.

It said it was working with global cybersecurity experts to "contain and secure the Coles IT environment".

Coles says no action needed by customers

Coles told investors and customers on Monday morning that it was business as usual for its operations.

"Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online," the company website said.

The supermarket group said customers do not need to take any action at this time but advised caution.

Woolworths probes reports of drained digital gift cards Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and is investigating, with replacement cards among the possible next steps for affected customers.

"We advise everyone to take basic online precautions and recommend remaining vigilant to suspicious links, attempts to solicit personal information from you — including by email, phone, text, or post — and potential scam activity," Coles said.

"We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reusing the same password across multiple services."

It urged similar caution from suppliers.

"We apologise for any concern this may cause our customers and key stakeholders at a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world," the company said.

In recent weeks, European supermarkets have been hit by IT incidents affecting fridge and freezer temperatures, which were believed to be cyber attacks.

Over the weekend, customers of Coles' major rival Woolworths reported digital gift cards being drained by unauthorised transactions. Woolworths told ABC News it was investigating.

A number of major Australian corporations have been rocked by cyber attacks and data breaches this year, including Origin Energy.

The hacking incident in July left about 900,000 current and former Origin customers' data exposed.

Coles said further updates would be provided "as appropriate".

title: Three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva stolen from Flemington
text:
The owner of legendary racehorse Makybe Diva says he is "totally devastated", after the mare's three Melbourne Cup trophies were stolen from Flemington Racecourse in Melbourne.

The cups had been on display at the racecourse for the Spring Racing Carnival since September.

Makybe Diva is the only horse to have won the famous race in three consecutive years, each time while being ridden by jockey Glen Boss.

The champion racehorse died earlier this year at the age of 27 after a short battle with the gastrointestinal condition colic.

Police are investigating the theft of three Melbourne Cup trophies won by Makybe Diva. (AAP: Julian Smith)

Tony Santic, who owned Makybe Diva, said he was "totally devastated".

"They were irreplaceable ... I just want them back in one piece," Santic said.

" Please just give the cups back. Put them somewhere and let the police know where they are and all's forgiven on my part. "

Santic said he was told two thieves broke into Flemington this morning, dressed like workers in high-vis clothing.

"At 8:30am the alarms went off, at 8:35 the cups were gone," Santic said.

He said the theft had added to the sadness of losing Makybe Diva.

"She was an icon in her own right, became known as 'The People's Horse', she achieved something no other horse has achieved.

" Looking after her for the last 23 years and she passed away in February and for this to happen, it just broke my heart. "

VRC 'devastated' by theft

This afternoon, Victoria Police issued as statement confirming the incident was being treated as a burglary and theft.

"It is believed three Melbourne Cup trophies were stolen from a cabinet, on Epsom Road," a police spokesperson said.

"An investigation into the incident is ongoing."

Former trainer David Hall, jockey Glen Boss and owner Tony Santic with Makybe Diva at Flemington Racecourse in 2025. (Supplied: Victoria Racing)

In its own statement, Victoria Racing Club said it was "devastated by the incident".

Two workers who were at the racecourse this morning said it looked like someone had used a glass cutter or similar equipment to break into the cabinet.

"Because the glass was on the outside [of the display], not the inside," one said.

They said they were not surprised to hear the thieves may have been dressed as tradies.

"They basically could have got anywhere with their high vis on and a ladder, that's all they needed," one said.

"They would have looked the part, for sure," added the other.

Police and the racing club have urged anyone who witnessed the theft, who has dashcam or CTV footage or any other information to contact Crime Stoppers.

title: Racehorse So You Are dies of colic 13 days after running in Melbourne Cup
text:
Australian racehorse So You Are has died from a "severe bout of colic", just 13 days after finishing eighth in the Melbourne Cup.

Trainer Bjorn Baker announced today that the five-year-old had been rushed to hospital with colic, which refers to abdominal pain in horses.

"We are devastated to share the news that So You Are has died following a severe bout of colic," the statement said.

"He had been enjoying a well-earned spell when he was found showing signs of colic this morning. He was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment, but sadly could not be saved.

"Beyond his achievements on the track, So You Are was a much-loved horse, and his loss will be deeply felt by everyone who knew and cared for him."

So You Are was trained by Baker at Warwick Farm in Sydney, and had a terrific spring where he won four times, including a trio of Group 3 races at Rosehill, Randwick and Bendigo.

He was owned by Stuart Ramsey, a long-time breeder and racehorse owner, and his wife Trish.

So You Are ran in the Melbourne Cup 13 days ago, finishing eighth in a race won by Point of Law.

So You Are was running second in the home straight with about 600 metres left in the race, leading the chase for long-time leader Royal Supremacy.

title: Microsoft unlikely to compensate for loss of productivity
text:
Millions of Australians were unable to use their Outlook emails during the Microsoft outage that spanned most of the day on Friday.

This halted business operations, interrupted workdays and made everyday online actions extremely difficult for many.

But if you're expecting to be compensated for the headaches the outage brought, don't expect a big cash payout.

Could we be compensated for the Microsoft outage?

Yes, but it will probably just be businesses, RMIT Associate Professor Mark Gregory says.

Dr Gregory says a service level agreement that businesses have with providers such as Microsoft will often have requirements that certain targets are met.

This could be something like the service being fully operational for 99.49 per cent of the year.

"Some of these agreements have mechanisms for compensation if the targets are not met," Dr Gregory says.

"The typical scenario though is that the compensation is in terms of returning a percentage of the monthly or annual fee for using that service.

"It doesn't normally extend to lost productivity."

Microsoft's agreements would only cover the loss of that service, but not the knock-on effects of that, Deakin IT lecturer Fariha Jaigirdar says.

"The loss of productivity is not something they are bound to compensate for," Dr Jaigirdar.

And this compensation is generally made in terms of a credit, which could equate to a small discount on the company's next bill.

"If people are expecting [that] cash will be in their account … that is not something that is going to happen," Dr Jaigirdar says.

It's unclear how Microsoft will address calls for compensation in the coming days, with the global nature of the outage putting pressure on the technology giant to repair its reputation.

The ABC has contacted Microsoft for comment.

How much could the credit be?

There isn't one dollar figure that would apply to every business, Dr Jaigirdar says

This all depends on how much a business pays for its Microsoft services.

And this also depends on whether a business can successfully file a compensation claim with Microsoft, which requires certain information to process compensation.

While larger companies with legal departments might have in-house experts to make a claim, the process could be tricky for smaller businesses to navigate, Dr Jaigirdar says.

"I don't think it's a very straightforward process," she says.

Credit won't cover losses

While a credit towards a monthly bill couldn't hurt, it could be a drop in the ocean compared with what some businesses lost on Friday.

"The credit is tiny compared with the loss of productivity," Dr Gregory says.

"It's a bit like when there's a telco outage, people ultimately just have to wear it and move on."

Dr Gregory says providers such as Microsoft might argue that it's up to businesses to sort out productivity insurance and have alternative workarounds during outages, but it's not that simple.

He says that may well be the case for preparing for things such as telecommunications outages, by having another SIM card, for example.

"[But] with IT and with software, it's not so easy," Dr Gregory says.

"It's not something that you can easily duplicate.

"That argument, to some extent, does not hold water."

Millions of people were unable to send or receive emails via Outlook on Friday. (ABC)

What could the ACCC do?

That's a good question.

"There is potential for the ACCC to weigh in on the matter, the problem is of course under what section of the act," Dr Gregory says.

There were changes to the legislation that permitted the ACCC to take action against companies that provide telecommunications services.

That legislation was fairly broad.

"[But] that would be in terms of a legal action over the outage, not in relation to compensation," Dr Gregory says.

What about a class action?

"It's a question of really what the purpose of the class action is and whether or not they would try to go beyond the loss of service compensation to loss of productively compensation," Dr Gregory says.

"There may be law firms that want to go to court to just see where the limits are.

"Sometimes this is positive because then it makes it clear about the strengths or weaknesses of current legislation."

The ABC is aware of at least one legal firm investigating the potential for a class action lawsuit over the outage.

Victoria Peak Litigation Funding is currently putting the call out for businesses and individuals who may have suffered financial losses as a result of the outage.

However, the firm is careful to stress that registering to take part "does not establish entitlement to compensation or mean that proceedings have commenced".

And even if a class action does get off the ground and is successful, it can take quite a while until participants see any money.

Calls for automated compensation

Dr Gregory says this saga highlights the need for tougher legislation about how people are compensated when big providers — such as Microsoft — fail.

"The Australian government does need to look at automated compensation," he says.

"But also strengthening sovereign capability so that things like outages outside Australia don't impact productivity inside Australia."

Compensation is likely to come in the form of a credit to your bill, so don't expect significant cash to be coming your way. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

While Dr Jaigirdar doesn't expect changes to be made to legislation overnight, she's hopeful it will prompt action.

"This is adding serious fuel to the regulatory fire in our country," she says.

"Platforms are no longer just office software, they are essential national infrastructure — no different from telecommunications and water.

"It needs to be taken seriously."

She also called for a national alert system to inform the community about similar outages in the future.

title: Two left stuck on Perth ferris wheel in the dark after ride turned off
text:
Two people have been rescued after being left stranded in the dark at the top of a giant ferris wheel in Perth's CBD when it was turned off on Saturday night.

The pair had been on the 36-metre-tall SkyVista ferris wheel at Langley Park when they were seemingly left in one of the ride's carriages when it closed for the evening.

They reportedly alerted passers-by below to their predicament by shining the torches from their mobile phones.

The pair were seemingly left in one of the ride's carriages. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Three firefighting trucks were sent to the SkyVista at 9:30pm and a combined ladder platform was erected to reach them and check they were safe.

The Department of Fire and Emergency Services (DFES) said it found two people "safely secured inside a carriage at the peak of the ferris wheel."

SkyVista is operated by Carnival Amusements and can carry up to 144 riders. (Instagram: SkyVista Observation Wheel)

It said the operators of SkyVista returned and lowered the pair back to the ground at 10:48pm.

"Crews worked with the ferris wheel operator to establish the safest rescue plan, which was for the operator to attend and lower the occupants," DFES said in a statement.

City of Perth rangers were also on the scene, but the SkyVista is independently run and not under the city's jurisdiction.

SkyVista is operated by Carnival Amusements, which has been contacted for comment, including about whether the operators turned off the ride with two people still in a carriage.

Loading Instagram content

Carnival Amusement's website said its giant ferris wheel had 24 gondolas and could carry up to 144 riders at a time, offering "breathtaking panoramic views you won't forget".

The company's managing director Mark Marinovich is quoted on its website as saying: "We handle the logistics, safety and compliance properly, so the day runs smoothly, and that reliability is why so many WA events book us back year after year."

title: Byron Bay girl stuns surfing world just days after turning 14
text:
Byron Bay surfing prodigy Leihani Zoric has made history in Peru, becoming the youngest woman to win the ISA Open Women's World Games title.

Her victory over a star-studded field that included former world professional champions Stephanie Gilmore, Tyler Wright and Carissa Moore came just days after she turned 14.

"I'm pretty amazed with my performance and the achievement," she said.

"There's so many great surfers that I got to surf against, so I'm just really grateful to have had that opportunity to get to push my surfing against the best girls in the world."

The teenager's road to the victory was anything but smooth.

A loss in Round 3 left her needing to win eight repechage heats to make the final.

"That was my first competition against [WSL] Championship Tour athletes," Zortic said.

"I was really excited because you watch them on the world [tour] charging and pushing the levels.

"I was like, 'All right, well I see how good they are, and I know that I reckon I can do this.'"

The 14-year-old enjoyed the support of her teammates as she led the Australian team to a dominant victory.

"Before I would paddle out for my heats, they would do a little tunnel and start [yelling] my name," she said.

"Then I'd go up and hit this sign every time that says 'the road to LA begins here' because that's my goal: to qualify for LA 28.

"It was really cool to have them cheering for me, especially before the finals, like everybody was so psyched up."

The competition was a qualifying event for the 2028 Olympics, and Zoric's win makes a strong case for her inclusion in the Australian team.

Leihani Zoric celebrating her win and her indigenous heritage. (ISA Jerrson Barboza)

"I do have a chance to qualify for it, but I think I have to get another really good result next year at another big event," she said.

" I want to go to LA 28 because LA stands for Leihani and Atlas: Atlas is my brother and best friend so it would mean so much to me to get to represent my country and family. "

Leihani Zoric during the final of the International Surfing Association event in Peru. (ISA Sean Evans)

President of the Byron Bay Boardriders Club Neil Cameron said rising star was "something special".

"I think she's probably surprised a lot of people, but she hasn't surprised a lot of us here in Byron Bay because we've seen what she's been doing for the last few years," he said.

"She's an amazing athlete and has all the necessary requirements to compete at a high level."

Mr Cameron credited Leihani's parents, Kirsty and Clay, with her level-headedness and drive to win.

"They've trained her since she's been about five years of age and I think they realised she had something special even from then," he said.

"They have put their life into Leihani, and it's been fortunate that they've lived right next to the ocean at Broken Head."

Mr Cameron said her capacity to thrive under pressure was rare in someone so young.

"We've seen that in her for a couple of years now, and that's something that not every surfer has," he said.

"Where she goes next will remain to be seen, and the parents will decide, I guess, where she goes from here.

" The world is her oyster at the moment, that's for sure. "

The young prodigy, who has also won Indigenous and world under-18 titles, has her sights set on breaking more records.

"I hope that I get a wild card into the Snapper Rocks [WSL event], that's my goal is to compete at home," she said.

"It's literally an hour up the road; I really want to be the youngest to ever win a Championship Tour event.

"I know that Tyler [Wright] is the youngest to ever win a CT event, so hopefully I can win that one day; that'd be pretty cool."

Queenslander Ethan Ewing took out the men's crown in a stunning day for Australian surfing.

Ewing delivered a star performance in his final, nailing a perfect 10-point ride, followed by a 9.17 to score a competition-high 19.17 points to defeat Peru's Lucca Mesinas and Miguel Tudela.

"It was a bit nerve-wracking going into the final," the 2024 Olympian said.

"Everyone had been surfing extremely well all week, but I think it really came down to who got the best waves.

"Halfway through my 10-point ride, I knew I was off and running. The wave just stood up so well and kept going."

title: Advice panel gives conditional OK to controversial puberty blockers
text:
Puberty blockers should remain a clinical option for certain trans and gender diverse children, despite low-certainty evidence about their benefits and harms, according to long-awaited national advice.

But Queensland and the Northern Territory have already rejected the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) interim advice, vowing to maintain their bans or restriction of puberty blockers in the public system.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues (GnRHa) or puberty blockers, are injections that pause aspects of physical development by suppressing sex hormones.

They are a form of medical intervention prescribed to children with gender incongruence, a clinical term for a difference between a person's gender and their sex recorded at birth.

Some people with gender incongruence also experience distress, which is known as gender dysphoria.

National guidelines on puberty blockers are due in 2028. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Advocates argue pausing puberty temporarily buys patients time to decide if they want to take the next steps towards transitioning with hormones like oestrogen or testosterone. However critics say the medication is experimental and potentially dangerous.

In 2025, Health Minister Mark Butler asked the NHMRC to develop national guidelines for the care of trans and gender diverse young people, including priority interim advice on puberty blockers.

The interim advice, released on Monday for public consultation, used what is known as the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, which rates the certainty of evidence and how strong a recommendation for or against a healthcare option should be.

The five types of recommendations under the GRADE approach: Strongly for: Benefits clearly outweigh the harms; recommended for most people.

Benefits clearly outweigh the harms; recommended for most people. Conditionally for : Benefits likely outweigh the harms; the best choice may depend on the individual patient.

: Benefits likely outweigh the harms; the best choice may depend on the individual patient. Conditional for either option : Neither option is clearly better than the other; either may be appropriate depending on the patient.

: Neither option is clearly better than the other; either may be appropriate depending on the patient. Conditionally against : Harms likely outweigh the benefits; treatment may be appropriate in some circumstances.

: Harms likely outweigh the benefits; treatment may be appropriate in some circumstances. Strongly against: Harms clearly outweigh the benefits; treatment is generally not recommended.

The Gender Guidelines Development Committee (GGDC) made a conditional recommendation for the use of the medication for certain young people.

It said conditional recommendations were more common than strong recommendations in clinical guidelines.

"A conditional recommendation is made in cases where shared decision-making is essential because different options may be appropriate for different individuals and they might make different choices, or where the overall certainty of available evidence is low. Both are the case here," the report said.

The committee suggested that based on a shared decision between the patient, their carers and clinicians, puberty blockers could be considered for a young person who had gender incongruence with or without distress, were assessed as suitable for treatment and had begun puberty.

Puberty blockers have been used since the 1980s to treat young children who go through puberty early. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"Not all young people will want or need the same intervention at the same time or age, and care that is in one young person's best interests may not suit another," the report said.

The NHMRC review included 15 non-randomised studies, most with follow-up of six months to two years.

The committee found that the overall certainty of evidence was low, with studies largely observational and generally short-term.

"Although the available evidence indicates that serious adverse events are rare, a young person using GnRH agonists should be monitored for signs or symptoms that may warrant additional investigations and management," the report said.

Puberty blockers have increasingly been the subject of fierce debate, with countries like the UK, Finland and many US states seeking to restrict its use. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The reviewers said the available evidence showed puberty blockers may improve psychosocial functioning and may reduce suicidality behaviours, and found no eligible evidence on the impact on fertility, fractures or other measures of bone health.

The advice isn't legally mandatory

The medication has increasingly been the subject of fierce debate, with countries including the UK and Finland, as well as many US states, seeking to restrict its use.

The New Zealand government introduced a ban on new prescriptions of puberty blockers for children with gender dysphoria last year, however the High Court recently ruled the regulations unlawful, meaning doctors can prescribe them again.

Queensland pause on puberty blockers for trans teenagers to continue The Queensland government says it made the decision after considering a 530-page independent review into the evidence surrounding the treatments.

Last year, Queensland became the first state in Australia to restrict access to puberty blockers for children with gender dysphoria who were not already on them in the public system.

The Northern Territory also banned puberty blockers in the public system for people under 18.

As it paused access to the medication, Queensland ordered an independent review by prominent psychiatrist Ruth Vine.

It found the evidence base about the use of puberty blockers for gender dysphoria and on the impact of fertility was limited, with evidence the medication could impact bone health in the short to medium term.

However, it found the effects were "reversible" and with proper oversight "there can be benefit for a young person" in accessing the medication.

The puberty blockers debate The fierce debate over puberty blockers has become a collision of science and politics. To try to address a fractured consensus, the federal government is attempting to lay the groundwork for a national standard.

The Queensland government said it would continue the pause until 2031, while awaiting the results of an upcoming UK trial known as PATHWAYS, which has been delayed because of safety concerns and legal challenges.

Because the NHMRC guidance is advisory rather than legally mandatory, states and territories can ultimately decide how they implement it.

Health Minister Mark Butler asked the NHMRC to develop national guidelines for the care of trans and gender diverse young people. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Mr Butler said he expected all states and territories to give proper consideration to the NHMRC's advice.

"I'm very confident that every state government, no matter their political persuasion, will consider the advice of our pre-eminent authority very closely. Whether that will lead to a change of policy by either the Queensland or NT government is really a matter for them," he said.

Mr Butler said the topic of puberty blockers attracted "heightened" debate and public commentary that was not "always helpful" and he hoped this advice would provide younger Australians with the greatest possible confidence that clinicians treating them are using the best clinical guidelines.

However, Queensland and the Northern Territory have both been quick to rule out any changes.

"The Queensland government has already undertaken an independent review and made a clear decision on the provision of these treatments in our public hospitals," Health Minister Tim Nicholls said.

"Our position remains unchanged, and we will continue to prioritise the health, safety and wellbeing of young Queenslanders."

A Northern Territory government spokesperson said its position was "unchanged".

"Our decision is consistent with Queensland, the United Kingdom and Finland, which have all taken a cautious approach," they said.

The Endocrine Society recently examined the use of puberty blockers for children who go through puberty early, known as precocious puberty.

The reviewers also made a conditional recommendation for the use of the medication, based on very low certainty evidence.

Why is there low certainty evidence?

Ethical and practical limitations around the way research is conducted, particularly when it comes to children, means high certainty evidence about puberty blockers is very difficult to obtain.

The gold standard of scientific studies is known as randomised controlled trials, which compares two groups randomly selected. One is given the treatment, and the other is given something else, like a placebo, or even the same treatment at a different time.

However, this approach raises ethical concerns when it comes to puberty blockers, because it can mean delaying or withholding treatment for children.

The medication has been the subject of fierce debate and is restricted in parts of Australia and overseas. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

In addition, double blind trials — where neither the participants nor researchers know who is receiving the treatment — are also off the table, because the drugs stop physical changes like menstruation, meaning people can guess if they are receiving them.

That has left a reliance on observational studies, where scientists observe individuals without manipulating the environment, however these are considered to be lower quality because without comparison, researchers cannot be sure what impact the treatment itself has had.

Proponents argue that low certainty evidence is very common for other areas of paediatrics, and does not mean an absence of evidence or evidence of harm.

But opponents interpret it as a reason for greater caution, saying the benefits have not been established with enough confidence to justify their use.

Critics have also condemned the lack of transparency about how many children are on puberty blockers nationwide.

Clinicians prescribing puberty blockers argue only a small portion of patients referred to gender clinics go on to take puberty blockers, however when the ABC approached every state and territory for the figures earlier this year, most declined to provide the information.

For the medication to be as effective as possible, it needs to be taken early in puberty.

However generally patients cannot access other medication, like hormones oestrogen or testosterone, until after they turn 16, while gender-affirming surgery is usually only available for adults.

The full national guidelines, covering broader clinical practice for the care of trans and gender diverse people under 18 who have gender dysphoria, will be released in 2028.

In April 2023, Travis Auld was left shattered after being overlooked for the biggest job in Australian rules football. Now, after swapping the AFL for Formula 1 and spending three years running the Australian Grand Prix, Auld is preparing to leave the country for a mysterious international business role he refuses to identify. AGPC chief executive officer Travis Auld is stepping down to take up a new role elsewhere. Eddie Jim The outgoing Australian Grand Prix Corporation CEO won’t reveal his next employer, the nature of the job or even which country he and his family are moving to. But in an exclusive interview with this masthead, Auld has opened up about the disappointment of missing out on the AFL chief executive position, the career gamble that followed and why he believes Melbourne will never lose hosting rights for the Formula 1 Grand Prix.

Advertisement

He also revealed ambitious plans for the Australian Grand Prix Corporation to expand beyond motor sport and pursue other major events. “I quickly moved on from the disappointment, I suppose, of not getting the [AFL] CEO role,” Auld said. “I felt like the one thing I could control is what I did next.” Auld spent almost 25 years in football, including senior roles at Essendon, Gold Coast and AFL headquarters, before emerging as a leading candidate to replace Gillon McLachlan in 2023. When Andrew Dillon won the race for the AFL’s top job, Auld faced a choice: remain in the industry he had known for most of his professional life or test himself elsewhere.

Advertisement

He chose the latter, taking charge of the Australian Grand Prix Corporation despite admitting he knew little about motor sport or the organisation he was joining. “When you spend most of your career in one sport … you do wonder the extent to which those skills are transferable,” he said. “I remember when I made a decision to leave the AFL industry, I wanted to test myself doing something different. “It’s always nice when you take a risk with a view in mind that this might lead to another opportunity, or you might just learn some new things, and that’s what it ends up being. It’s pretty rewarding.” Asked whether he was now glad he had missed out on the AFL job, Auld was philosophical.

Advertisement

“I don’t know if you’re ever glad that you missed out on a job,” he said. “I’m still incredibly grateful for the experience I had, and I wouldn’t change a thing.” His next move will take him overseas with his family, completing a career transformation from an AFL administrator to an executive working on the international stage. Lando Norris in action during the Australian Grand Prix in early March. Getty Auld said his time in motor sport had exposed him to a vastly different commercial environment, with international stakeholders, a rapidly changing fan base and an extraordinary pace of innovation. “The biggest difference is just the field you play on is a lot bigger in motor sport. It’s truly a global sport,” he said.

Advertisement

“The partners are different, the demographic’s very different, the pace of innovation is very different.” Auld will leave the grand prix corporation confident in its future, revealing plans for the organisation to expand its operations beyond Formula 1 and MotoGP. “There’s an exciting plan in place for this organisation to broaden its reach in terms of hosting other events, in and out of motor sport,” he said. “We’ve obviously just signed up Supercars, but I think there’s an opportunity to broaden that beyond motor sport.” He also delivered an emphatic defence of Melbourne’s right to host the Australian Formula 1 Grand Prix, dismissing suggestions the event could eventually be relocated to another Australian city.

Advertisement

Asked whether he could envisage the race leaving Melbourne in his lifetime, Auld replied: “No, I can’t. I can’t.” The Victorian government has secured the event until at least 2037, and Auld believed the city’s major-events culture, infrastructure and international reputation made it almost impossible to replace. “If we’ve got to host an event somewhere in Australia, it’s pretty hard to beat Melbourne,” he said. He also rejected criticism of the taxpayer investment required to stage the event, arguing the economic and tourism benefits comfortably justified the cost. Auld revealed the Saturday night of the 2026 staging of the grand prix had delivered Melbourne’s highest hotel occupancy on record, while the event continued to attract international visitors and showcase Victoria to a global audience.

Advertisement

“There are countries all around the world queuing up to get a Formula 1 race and we’ve got one through to 2037 at least,” he said. “I’m really comfortable that, from an economic and social perspective, the numbers well and truly justify the investment.” The AGPC confirmed interim leadership arrangements would be announced in “due course”, and chairman Martin Pakula said Auld would be a tough act to follow. “Under Travis’ leadership, the Formula 1 Australian Grand Prix has continued to strengthen its position as one of the world’s great major events, while AGPC has continued to grow its capability and ambition as a major events organisation,” he said. “Travis will be a hard act to follow, which is why the board is undertaking a comprehensive process to identify the very best person to lead AGPC into the future.”

Advertisement

Auld’s tenure has not been without challenges, including the cancellation of the final Phillip Island MotoGP race after severe weather prevented a medical evacuation helicopter from operating safely. As the search for his successor begins, Auld said the ability to remain composed under pressure would be essential. “Major events are, by their very nature, chaotic,” he said. “You have to enjoy the challenge that comes with dealing with a lot of issues at once … and create a sense of calmness amongst the chaos.” And while Auld is preparing to leave Australian sport behind, he has finally rediscovered something he lost during his years at AFL headquarters: the simple pleasure of watching football as a fan.

Health Minister Mark Butler has challenged states and territories that have banned puberty blockers for children to comply with new national guidelines, which suggest gender-diverse teens should get access to the treatment. The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) released an interim recommendation on Monday after the federal government launched a landmark review into the medical treatment of transgender children and adolescents in January 2025. Labor moved swiftly to interrogate the prescription of gender transition drugs, including puberty blockers, for young people after Queensland banned them, following the United Kingdom after a health service commission found there was little scientific evidence to support the treatment. Health Minister Mark Butler. Alex Ellinghausen The NHMRC recommended puberty blockers, or suppressants that delay hormonal development, be permitted across Australia for children whose gender-identity and sex recorded at birth don’t match. Prescriptions would have to be made in consultation with clinicians and parents as children begin to show physical signs of puberty.

Advertisement

The guideline does not require a diagnosis of gender dysphoria, the psychological distress about a mismatch of gender identity, to get treatment. The review acknowledged the low-certainty evidence for puberty blockers, but said guidelines must be provided for best practice. It noted the treatments were reversible. The council’s recommendation puts the Liberal government in Queensland and the Northern Territory, where bans on puberty blockers are in place, at odds with national guidelines, though the recommendation is not enforceable. Butler said all state governments had a responsibility to ensure the highest-quality care for all Australians. “I’m very confident that those state governments running these services will consider this advice very closely and make sure that their services are aligning with it,” Butler told reporters in Canberra.

Advertisement

Related Article Gender Puberty blockers and treatments for trans youth under review “I know traditionally, state governments of both political persuasions have always paid high regard to the advice of the National Health and Medical Research Council.” Butler emphasised the “unimpeachable reputation” of the NHMRC, which has set medical guidelines for decades. But those calling for a ban say there is not enough evidence the treatment is safe. “I have the utmost respect for the National Health and Medical Research Council, and I think the role that it has long played in this country at arm’s length from the government of the day and the political process to provide the highest quality clinical advice to health practitioners and the community generally should always be respected,” Butler said. “That’s why I asked them to try and review the evidence, and issue some pre-eminent guidelines to guide this contested, evolving area that’s the subject of so much public commentary and involves some of our most vulnerable members of the community.”

Advertisement

Queensland’s health minister, Tim Nicholls, rejected the new guidelines, saying the state government had made a clear decision on the provision of treatment based on its own independent review. “Our position remains unchanged, and we will continue to prioritise the health, safety and wellbeing of young Queenslanders,” he said. The state’s LNP government announced a ban in January last year on all publicly funded hormone treatments, including puberty blockers, for children under 18. The ban sparked a legal brawl between the parent of a transgender teenager and the government, with Nicholls using his ministerial powers to reinstate the ban after a Supreme Court judge ruled in favour of the parent. A class action against the ban was also launched in June.

Advertisement

New Zealand’s High Court last month struck down the national ban on puberty blockers, ruling that it amounted to unjustified discrimination and had not been subject to sufficient consultation. Butler on Monday acknowledged the UK Cass review had sharpened public debate in Australia. But he said the UK context was different, and was influenced by “pretty questionable private prescribing practices” and a less multidisciplinary model of care to Australia. The nation’s largest gender clinic, in Melbourne, prescribed 64 young people puberty suppressants in eight years, with an average wait of 530 days, Butler said. The NHMRC advice on puberty blockers is an interim guideline ahead of its broader recommendations on gender-affirming care such as the prescription of hormones, expected in 2028.

Critical Resources has secured a land access agreement for its Mayview antimony-gold prospect in New South Wales, finally clearing the way for boots-on-the-ground exploration of historic workings that previously delivered stunning rock chip grades of up to 52.3 per cent antimony. With access now approved by the local landholder, the company can begin a low-impact exploration program of soil and rock chip sampling, along with detailed geological mapping over some 270 metres of known historic workings. Critical Resources’ Halls Peak project area, which contains the Mayview prospect, is just 2.7km from Larvotto Resources’ Hillgrove antimony-gold operations in New South Wales. Previous rock chip sampling from historic workings and waste dumps at Mayview returned a suite of impressive results, including the headline 52.3 per cent antimony hit. Other samples recorded up to 38.3 per cent antimony, while another sample delivered a solid combination of 15.35 per cent antimony and 2.71 grams per tonne (g/t) gold. Further encouraging results include one hit of 12.45 per cent antimony and 2.18g/t gold alongside a second rock chip that registered 11.2 per cent antimony and 1.13g/t gold.

Significantly, Mayview lies just 2.7 kilometres from Larvotto Resources’ major Hillgrove antimony-gold project. Nearby Hillgrove is being developed as a significant new non-China source, with Larvotto forecasting annual production of 4900 tonnes of antimony and 40,500 ounces of gold over an initial eight-year mine life. The company says that regional development adds weight to the geological significance of Mayview, where historic antimony-gold workings could be part of the same mineral-rich system that hosts Hillgrove, potentially extending southeast into Critical’s ground. The on-ground work is designed to give Critical the data it needs to define and rank drill targets for a potential maiden campaign. Any drilling campaign would require a further access agreement. Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “Mayview has returned some of the highest antimony grades we have seen at Halls Peak, and securing land access means we can now start the work needed to understand what sits beneath those historic workings.” *

The Mayview program comes as antimony has gained strategic importance following China’s export restrictions and a tightening global supply picture. As early-stage work in NSW gets underway, it represents only one part of the company’s multi-pronged global strategy. Critical’s other critical metals asset is its Mavis Lake lithium project in Ontario, Canada, where it has already defined a significant inferred mineral resource of eight million tonnes grading a solid 1.07 per cent lithium oxide. It is also undertaking grassroots exploration at its nearby Vermillion Bay lithium project. Notably, the company has also recently made an aggressive push into South American gold, securing a significant 228-square-kilometre ground package in Suriname. The portfolio includes three projects, Gadu Manda, Gonini and Greenstars, all sitting in the highly prospective Guiana Shield. The geological province is considered the South American counterpart to West Africa’s phenomenally rich Birimian Shield, home to 500 million ounces of discovered gold. The sizzle in Critical’s Suriname play is the nearology. Its Gadu Manda project lies just 4km from Chinese giant Zijin Mining’s 11.6-million-ounce Rosebel mine, a monster operation that has produced more than six million ounces of gold. More recently, gold giant Gold Fields tipped C$77 million (A$80M) into explorer Founders Metals for a 19.9 per cent stake and private investment house La Mancha took significant positions in other Canadian-listed explorers active in Suriname.

China, which dominates global production, tightened the export screws in 2024, sending prices soaring and leaving international buyers scrambling for alternative supplies. An “angry” Premier Ben Carroll has instructed government departments to stop their controversial obstruction of the Big Build royal commission, as a senior minister stood beside him to publicly deny suggestions from her old agency that she was briefed about CFMEU disruptions on a key project. A self-described “birth keeper” advised an expectant mother to “go home and rest” after two doctors told her to urgently present to the emergency department, the NSW Coroner’s Court has heard. Sita Kali – also known as Mumma Sita – was involved in the care of two of the four babies who died following a “free-birth” or homebirth in the NSW Northern Rivers region between 2022 and 2024. ‘Birth keeper’ Sita Kali was involved in the free-births of two babies who died in the Northern Rivers region. These four deaths are being examined at an inquest which started at Lismore Local Court on Monday. The families of the four babies who died declined to be involved in the inquest. The small but growing number of free-births fall entirely outside the medical system. As opposed to a planned midwife-led homebirth, a free birth mother may be alone, with a partner or unaccredited support person such as a doula or birth keeper.

Kali is based in the Byron region. Kali described her role as “a birth keeper [who] provides advice which allows women to make informed decisions as to the best way to birth their children”, the court heard. She does not carry any medical equipment that could assist women in a medical emergency. The court heard about a woman who had a “very strong desire” to homebirth but was out of area for her local hospital’s homebirth program. The woman instead planned to free birth with Kali and a doula. While midwives had estimated the woman’s due date was July 28, 2022, based on the scientifically proven method of calculating a due date based on her last period, Kali estimated a due date weeks later, on August 14 or 15, based on the likely date of conception. The woman did not give birth until 43 weeks and one day gestation, and the court heard Kali “played a critical and crucial role into altering [the mother’s] understanding as to when her baby was due”.

Advertisement

On August 18, the mother was “getting a little worried about being late on the hospital calculation”, however given she was “only one week after the date that Sita calculated … I felt OK”, the court heard. She attended an ultrasound on August 19, which found the baby had a very compromised heart rate, prompting the radiologist to urgently call her GP who contacted the mother to express his concern. Both doctors explained to the mother that her pregnancy had become a medical emergency which required a heartbeat monitor and birth within four hours. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Inside freebirthing: Empowerment, distrust and a growing dogma The mother said she was afraid of being “forced into a caesarean” if she attended hospital, and called Kali for advice.

Advertisement

“I advised [the mother] to go home and rest, calm herself down and consider what she wanted to do,” Kali said in her police statement. “My advice was that I wasn’t medically trained.” The baby was delivered on August 20 just after 8am, with the father, Kali and the doula present. The baby’s skin was white, had the umbilical cord wrapped twice around his neck, was not breathing and had faeces on his face. There was difficulty establishing breathing for a few minutes, but breathing returned following massage. Loading The mother had a preference for a lotus birth, which involves allowing an umbilical cord to dry and detach naturally, usually three to ten days after birth. The umbilical cord was still attached when paramedics arrived 12 hours later.

Advertisement

Kali recorded that the baby displayed signs of laboured breathing, but told the mother that holding him close to her chest would help. The pair discussed going to hospital, but decided it was not needed. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘These are avoidable’: Dozens of babies dead or permanently injured after freebirths Kali left before the baby had latched to feed, and the court heard that the baby never latched. In the evening, the baby developed hiccups and stopped breathing about five minutes later. Paramedics arrived just before 11pm, where they found a limp and hypoxic baby with a heart rate of over 100.

Advertisement

A number of attempts were made to intubate, but the baby was pronounced dead just after midnight. The baby’s father told police that in the brief time he was with them, he gave them love, and that he does not know or care about the baby’s cause of death. Kali has launched an online fundraising campaign to assist with her legal fees and had raised $4500 of her $15,000 goal on Monday. “My journey began with my own first birth, on the side of a mountain more than 26 years ago,” Kali’s fundraising site read. “That experience profoundly shaped my understanding of birth as a natural, physiological, emotional and spiritual process, and awakened a lifelong calling to support wombyn [sic] in reclaiming trust in their bodies, their instincts and their right to make informed choices.”

Locksley Resources has given its Greater Tottenham copper-gold project in central New South Wales a serious shot in the arm, unveiling an updated mineral resource of 10 million tonnes (Mt) at 1.10 per cent copper and 0.32 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 110,000 tonnes of contained copper and 100,000 ounces of gold. Notably, the new estimate represents a whopping 56 per cent jump in copper grade and a hefty 37 per cent lift in contained copper compared to the previous 2022 resource. Gold also joined the party, delivering a 36 per cent increase in grade and an 18 per cent boost in contained ounces, reflecting revised geological models, higher cut-off grades and pit-constrained reporting. The historic Carolina mine at Locksley Resources’ Greater Tottenham project in central NSW’s Cobar-Girilambone district. The updated resource consolidates three deposits, Mt Royal, Carolina and the Iron Duke prospect, into a single cohesive estimate. The work also boosts a portion of the resource into the higher-confidence indicated category for the first time. The Carolina deposit stands out as the highest-grade component, with its open-pit resource delivering 2.4Mt at a solid 1.22 per cent copper and 0.38g/t gold. The company says the deposit remains open down-plunge and to the north, offering the potential for further resource upgrades. The combined Carolina and Mt Royal deposits now host a combined 8.9Mt at 1.09 per cent copper and 0.27g/t gold.

The campaign will target a 150-metre gap south of the existing resource in addition to infill and extensional drilling. Iron Duke is the most gold-rich of the three deposits, hosting a freshly updated inferred resource weighing in at 1.1Mt at 1.11 per cent copper and a healthy 0.61g/t gold. At the same time, the company is preparing a bigger 10,000-metre drill program for its Carolina and Mount Royal-Orange Plains prospects within the main Tottenham exploration licence to test sparsely drilled areas and chase extensions to known high-grade mineralisation. Adding another layer of blue-sky potential is the newly granted “Tottenham West” exploration licence. The ground adds 139 square kilometres to the portfolio and, more importantly, locks up an interpreted 10km-long structural trend with no historical drilling. The big resource upgrade clocks a key milestone in Locksley’s strategy of district-scale consolidation, having assembled a commanding 1000-square-kilometre land package within the Cobar Basin and Lachlan Orogen, home to major operations such as Tritton, CSA and the giant Cadia Valley operations. The NSW State Government has also recognised the region as prime copper country, with its Critical Minerals Strategy identifying copper as one of its five priority metals needed to meet the massive demand from global electrification and the energy transition.

title: One router, one bug. How routine upgrades caused worldwide chaos
text:
Advertisement

Analysis TechnologyNetwork outage One router, one bug. How routine upgrades caused worldwide chaos David Swan November 16, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Microsoft wanted more capacity. America’s aviation regulator wanted to swap ageing copper cables for fibre. Last week, both got chaos. Microsoft’s email and office software went dark for millions of people from shortly before 5am AEDT on Friday, after an upgrade meant to add capacity. A day later, US authorities grounded every departing flight in the country for five hours after a contractor installed a router at a remote site in Arkansas. Microsoft’s email and office software crashed after an upgrade meant to add capacity. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth The two failures were unrelated and Microsoft says it has no indication its services played any part in the grounding. The upgrades themselves were defensible: old systems commonly have to be replaced, and software has to be patched – that’s normal. What failed was containment: one fault in one place was allowed to course through an entire network.

Advertisement

Australians felt it within hours. ASIO and the federal police lost email and so did councils, courts and schools. Australia Post pulled its phone payment system, while suppliers couldn’t tell supermarket distribution centres what was on the way. In Germany, 15 hotel guests were reportedly hurt by chlorine gas after a pool safety system that sent its warnings by email went silent. A tech company like Microsoft understands the risk as well as anyone. “There are no low-risk deployments to production,” its guidance to engineers warns, meaning no change to a live system is ever truly safe. Its advice is to change things in small steps, roll them out slowly, and stop at the first wobble. Microsoft has apologised over the global outage. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson On Friday the company said the outage “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” after a later network change. Its preliminary notices say traffic moved around during that maintenance and exposed a hidden bug in the systems that connect people to their mailboxes. Requests banked up until the servers choked. Then the dominoes fell. Work from the broken servers spilled onto healthy ones, which buckled in turn. Even servers that engineers revived “can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic”, Microsoft warned. Turning it off and on again took the best part of two days.

Advertisement

The flight grounding was similar: it started with a single router in El Dorado, Arkansas. Contractor L3Harris was installing it as part of a job replacing old copper communication lines with fibre. According to the Federal Aviation Administration, a flood of connection attempts then scrambled radio and radar feeds to 17 of the 22 US centres that guide planes between airports. That’s more than three-quarters of the system, toppled from one small site. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the routers “got overloaded with data”. Investigators haven’t yet established whether faulty equipment or a slip during installation was to blame. Flight tracker FlightAware counted about 9800 delays and more than 4700 cancellations, and US-bound flights from Sydney were held on the ground. Flights were grounded across the US. CNN Dr Mohammad Goudarzi, who researches cloud computing at Monash University, said the chaos stemmed from misaligned priorities. “Investment in reliability needs to keep pace with investment in new features,” he said.

Advertisement

Related Article Network outage Microsoft’s global outage and fixes: What we know The immediate question now for Australian businesses is who pays. Microsoft customers may be able to claim service credits, the small refunds written into their contracts. Prins Ralston, chief executive of the Australian Computer Society, the technology profession’s peak body, said those credits “won’t make up for a lost morning of trade for a small business”. A litigation funder, Victoria Peak, is already inviting affected Australian businesses to register for a possible class action, though no case has been filed. Ralston said there was a clear difference between who coped and who didn’t. “ASIO and the AFP had workarounds. Most small businesses and many agencies don’t,” he said.

Advertisement

Microsoft has promised a full post-incident report. Every Australian board should read it with one question of its own: when the next upgrade goes wrong, what still works? The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

title: What Anthony Albanese's fried chicken move could signal to the world
text:
In brief Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has celebrated the upcoming launch of Filipino fast food chain Jollibee in Australia.

Some social media users expressed confusion about a video the prime minister posted supporting the chain.

While Anthony Albanese's promotion of a Filipino fast food chain has raised some eyebrows online, experts say the prime minister's fried chicken meal could strengthen ties with a regional ally.

Filipino fast food giant Jollibee is set to open in Australia — and the prime minister has celebrated the move in Manila with the company's president and CEO Ernesto Tanmantiong.

The chain, well-known in the Philippines for its fried chicken, operates more than 1,600 stores worldwide and aims to open 35 in NSW and Victoria over five years.

The Australian outlets are expected to create 900 direct jobs.

Albanese, who is in Manila for the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), said he wants to see "more businesses choose Australia as a place to grow and succeed".

He welcomed Jollibee as a "great example of the cultural connections that strengthen our relationship with the Philippines".

More than 400,000 people living in Australia were born in the Philippines, making it the country's fifth-largest diaspora community.

In a video posted to Albanese's Instagram, the prime minister celebrated with Jollibee staff and ate a meal at the fast food chain.

Concern about the PM's post

However, some social media users expressed confusion about the post and Albanese's endorsement of the chain, with one user commenting, "So, are you getting paid for this? Thought it was AI when I first saw it and can't believe it's for real."

Comedian and media personality Ben Sorensen commented on Albanese's video asking: "Was this a sponsored post?"

Politicians highlighting small businesses and large employers around Australia during election periods is extremely common, according to Emily Foley, a research fellow at the University of Canberra.

However, Foley told SBS News she hasn't seen this in a foreign affairs context before.

"I wouldn't say it's particularly common," she said.

Anne Nalder, founder and CEO of the Small Business Association of Australia, told SBS News the prime minister's promotion of Jollibee was "disappointing" at a time when small businesses in the food industry are "barely surviving" due to high costs.

Nalder also noted that around a third of small businesses in Australia are run by migrants.

"There's nothing wrong with an overseas company coming into Australia ... the thing about it is, I would like to see [the prime minister] concentrating on supporting Australian businesses because they need all the support they can get," she said.

A political calculation

Foley said there aren't any rules for politicians that would restrict a post like Albanese's, and his decision to post it likely comes down to a political calculation about appealing to Australia's Filipino diaspora.

"There is a bit of a grappling about what is acceptable for politicians to put on social media and the public sphere, but I don't think there's anything in particular that's necessarily frowned upon [in this case]," Foley said.

Whilst attracting critical comments, Albanese's video also received many supportive responses and attracted over 71,000 likes.

This is also not the first time the prime minister has encouraged a foreign business to enter Australia. During a meeting in the United Arab Emirates in 2025, Albanese visited a Lulu Hypermarket store — one of the largest retail chains in the Middle East, with over 250 stores across the region.

Albanese said at the time he had a discussion with Lulu Hypermarket chair Yusuff Ali as they walked around the store and invited the company to bring more competition to Australia's supermarket sector.

"They are the largest throughout the Middle East. Egypt, here ... the second-largest in Saudi Arabia," Albanese said.

"We know that Aldi, of course, has come to Australia, but this is a significant player that has an engagement with Australia, and I want to see that competition."

However, no plans have been announced for Lulu Hypermarket to enter the Australian market.

Fried chicken diplomacy

On Sunday, the Philippines and Australia signed a defence pact, strengthening ties between the two nations, which have grown over the past decade.

The agreement will step up maritime training and activities amid shared security concerns about China's growing militarisation of the South China Sea, particularly in an area deemed part of Filipino territorial waters by a UN arbitration in 2016.

Australia has taken part in 12 joint patrols with the Philippines in the South China Sea, with four in the last year.

However, Albanese insisted the defence agreement was not aimed specifically at any one country.

"This is about supporting the sovereignty of every country," he said.

READ MORE Australia to ink Philippines defence pact before Quad meeting with Donald Trump

While supporting the fried chicken chain is a demonstration of softer diplomacy than a defence pact, emeritus professor Paul Hutchcroft told SBS News the prime minister was likely trying to forge a connection between Australia and the Philippines.

"Jollibee is a source of pride for many Filipinos, competing successfully at home with American fast-food chains while also expanding overseas," he said.

"I can imagine that the PM was tapping into that sense of pride as a way of connecting with citizens of an important Australian ally."

Foley said Albanese's support of Jollibee has "interesting" foreign affairs implications as it highlights a "non-US, non-Western style business that's coming into Australia".

"It obviously speaks to the Labor government's real focus on trying to engage more with the Indo-Pacific, in particular highlighting things like ASEAN centrality — the kind of push to focus more on the political, economic and social ties and connections with neighbouring regional partners, rather than necessarily with the US."

title: Australians' shifting attitudes towards this emerging technology revealed
text:
in brief The federal goverment is looking to develop AI policy in order to attract investment.

Australians are becoming increasingly wary about artificial intelligence as the use of the technology grows more entrenched.

title: You may be eligible for a slice of Australia's missing $6 billion superannuation pie
text:
in brief Over three million Australians were reportedly underpaid a collective $6.3 billion in superannuation in 2023-24.

The CEO of the Super Members Council, which is behind that estimate, says "there is much more work to do".

More than $1.1 billion in unpaid superannuation has been returned to Australian workers over the past year, but millions of Australians may still be missing money they are legally owed.

New figures from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) show that the money was returned to the super accounts of more than 900,000 Australians.

The ATO also collected more than $1.1 billion in Super Guarantee Charge liabilities, up from $795 million in the previous financial year.

The enforcement action is encouraging, but the scale of unpaid super remains in the billions of dollars a year, Super Members Council CEO Misha Schubert said.

"Returning more than $1 billion in unpaid super to Australians is welcome progress. This is money owed to working Australians that is finally being paid to them," Schubert said.

title: US aviation shutdown may have been due to a faulty router, Trump admin says
text:
In brief The halt was declared after upgrade work on an old copper wire caused "issues" with communication with airplanes.

The ground stop raised serious concerns about the country's ageing infrastructure.

A massive, nearly five-hour shutdown of the US aviation system that disrupted more than 20,000 flights may have been the fault of a single router installed by government contractor L3Harris.

The incident is the latest painful example of the ageing US air traffic control ‌telecom system and the struggles to replace systems while keeping the old communications working.

In recent years, the Federal Aviation Administration's ageing systems have failed after errant fibre cuts, accidental file deletions, and a strong chemical smell caused by a melted component. The system will fail again until it is properly upgraded, government officials said.

"This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment," US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said ‌on Sunday AEDT.

Duffy said on Friday L3Harris was conducting routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fibre at at least one remote location.

L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and was "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop ‌of our nation's air travel".

L3 ‌noted it has completed more ⁠than 70 per cent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fibre-optic system.

"We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job," Duffy said, noting that "virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fibre, from analog to digital".
