title: Eurovision Song Contest Asia crowns its first-ever winner
text:
In brief The Asian version of Eurovision has been in the works since about 2009.

Philippines took home the winner's trophy, with Thailand finishing a close second.

A teenage pop star from the Philippines won the first Asia edition of Eurovision overnight after a night of power ballads, pop-dance hits and pyrotechnics from the makers of the cult European kitsch fest.

Carmelle, 19, was crowned queen of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok for her performance of Sobra-Sobra (Too Much), a shoutout to strong women.

Hosts Thailand finished a close second, followed by Vietnam, Malaysia and Laos, with Nepal, Cambodia and Bangladesh at the bottom of the points table.

Eleven countries joined the competition that organisers hope will start a new chapter for Eurovision, a cultural phenomenon in Europe for its lavish outfits, soaring vocals — and sometimes tricky geopolitics.

An Asian version has been in the works since about 2009 and SBS had a hand in trying to launch it around 2017 before shelving it in 2025. The European Broadcasting Union, which organises Eurovision, later announced the contest in March.

"I'm genuinely impressed with what they've done, the vibe and the music," said Alex Cobham, 33, a British Eurovision fan who lives in Thailand and could not believe her luck when it was staged in Bangkok.

"It's embodying the spirit for sure — camp, fun, gorgeous, good songs."

Eurovision is the world's biggest televised live music event, drawing 131 million viewers in 2026, and over the past 70 years has helped to launch the careers of global superstars such as ABBA and Celine Dion.

But the big question is whether it can take off in Asia, the world's most populous region with more than enough music shows of its own.

The audience was small in Bangkok on Saturday (local time) but the energy was big, with the international crowd going wild for Thailand's pop duo Mang x Daou and South Korea's K-pop star Junhee.

Thailand's contestants Mang x Daou perform during the grand final. Source: AFP / Chanakarn Laosarakham

"I'm very pleased it's come to Asia. We've been waiting so long!" said Malaysian mega-fan Fauzan, 37, one of the first in line for the show.

He was wearing a blue corset over a white trouser suit in honour of his nation's entry Aina Abdul, who performed her song inside a giant water droplet wearing a dress that took 600 hours to make.

She was an early favourite after juries from participating countries cast their votes, but Carmelle shot ahead on the public vote.

"This is such an unexpected journey for me," the singer said afterwards, brandishing her trophy, admitting she did not know about Eurovision before.

Philippines' contestant Carmelle (2nd from right) said her performance of Sobra-Sobra was a shoutout to strong women. Source: AFP / Chanakarn Laosarakham

"I really enjoyed it. I feel like it's not a competition, I feel like I just did my own concert," she said.

In her song, Carmelle declares that anyone who says she is too much for them is not enough for her.

It's a "tribute to all the Filipino women", she said.

Spectacular staging is a hallmark of Eurovision but budgets were tight in Bangkok, so most performers relied on smoke, flares and eye-catching visuals.

There were deeply heartfelt performances but also a lot of fun, including the use of multi-coloured tuk-tuks — the symbol of Bangkok — to ferry contestants on stage.

Singing must be live under Eurovision rules and some of the performers struggled, but the producers ramped up the energy, with a pop track by Vietnam's Toc Tien morphing into a heavy dance tune.

The Asia edition was organised by commercial television — unlike Eurovision, which is run by national broadcasters — and the contestants were mostly well known in their home countries.

But some have a less typical background, including Mongolian singer Beck, a trained economist who advises his country's deputy prime minister.

Bhutan's Nyendra, a 24-year-old singer-songwriter who had never before left his home country, admitted that "nobody knows me".

Eurovision marks its 70th birthday this year under a cloud, with 2026 viewing figures down 35 million on-year after a boycott by five countries over Israel's participation.

Organisers brush off any link between this controversy and the Asia show, noting the contest has been trying to expand for years. There was a US version in 2022, but it fell flat.

India, Japan and China were notably absent at Saturday's contest, but organisers hope to get them on board at a later date.

Martin Green, director of the European Broadcasting Union, said it could take "two, three, five years" to establish the brand.

"Eurovision number one was basically with seven singers doing two songs each with a pot plant and a microphone," he told reporters, saying Saturday's show was "profoundly not the case".

title: Why Australians could face cybersecurity risks in the wake of the Microsoft outage
text:
In Brief Organisations scrambling to keep working during the outage may have caused a major cybersecurity risk, experts say.

About 79 per cent of Australian consumers want stronger protections for online services.

Australia's peak cybersecurity body fears an enormous amount of sensitive information may have bypassed normal security walls during a day-long Microsoft outage.

Global disruption of the company's Outlook and Teams finally eased on Saturday after about 24 hours of chaos that crippled online communications.

The mass outage forced some ‌organisations to revert to fax and halted at least one European bond repurchase.

Described as a disaster for the Australian business sector, it has deepened questions about global reliance on a handful of major tech companies supplying essential software and the cloud infrastructure underpinning it.

The Australian Information Security Association (AISA) said organisations scrambling to keep working during the outage using personal email accounts, USB drives and other alternative platforms may have caused a major cybersecurity risk.

"When people can't access the systems they rely on, they find ways to keep working," AISA board director Doctor Rajiv Shah said.

"Given the massive number of organisations affected around the world, we could be looking at an enormous amount of information that has moved outside normal security arrangements in a single day," he said.

"We need to understand how much additional cyber risk has been created."

Billions potentially lost

It mounts more pressure on Australian businesses feared to have lost billions of dollars within only 12 hours of the shutdown, according to Ashwin Pal from accounting firm RSM Australia.

"That's not just direct but indirect costs as well," he said.

"A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel's back for smaller entities."

He said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans but many businesses didn't have a fallback.

"They're just at a standstill — if you don't actually have a plan B, then you've got a problem," he said.

Shah said businesses needed to build greater redundancy, such as independent communication channels, offline access to critical information and alternative ways to authenticate users in case of a major outage.

The Australian Computer Society renewed its call for a national review of sovereign risk in Australian IT, whilst Australian consumer groups said the outage highlighted a need for stronger complaints systems.

"Australians who couldn't get paid, couldn't send an invoice or couldn't reach a government service are entitled to be worried," chief executive of Computer Society Prins Ralston said.

"Where were the direct updates to Australian customers and media — and who will answer for the lost productivity and the cost to the economy?"

According to research by the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network, consumer trust in big tech is at an all time low with many feeling trapped using platforms they find hard to move from.

About 79 per cent of consumers want stronger protections for online services while 81 per cent say the apps they use are important to their day-to-day life.

title: The science behind Anthony Albanese's unusual hot mic moment
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen were overheard discussing concerns about the impact of phones on health.

Researchers have examined the effects of electromagnetic radiation on human organs.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was caught on a hot mic joking with Energy Minister Chris Bowen about phone radiation and penises at the COP31 climate summit.

The prime minister was recorded speaking to Bowen on Friday evening as they waited for a roundtable discussion to begin in Antalya, Türkiye.

"Do you keep your phone here? Don't," Albanese cautioned Bowen, gesturing to his left breast pocket, sparking an exchange about the potential impact of mobile phones on the body, including the heart's rhythm.

"I'm more conscious ... I've stopped putting it in my pants pocket," Bowen began before Albanese interrupted.

"Because of your d--k," the prime minister said.

"It's rather important — arguably more important than the heart," Bowen replied as the pair laughed.

Channel Seven initially broadcast a clip of their private banter on Friday evening.

A spokesperson for Albanese downplayed the leaked moment, saying the pair "were having a joke in between meetings," according to Nine newspapers.

However, the joking exchange raises questions about the impact of mobile phones on health, including common concerns they can cause cancer.

Can phones affect your organs and health?

A large number of studies have investigated these links, with some studies raising concerns and others finding little convincing evidence of harm.

The current available research does not indicate using a mobile phone is associated with harmful health effects, according to the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA).

Mobile phones emit radiofrequency electromagnetic fields (EMF), a form of non-ionising radiation.

Unlike ionising radiation, such as X-rays, this type of radiation does not have enough energy to directly damage DNA.

Research published in 2024 led by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) looked at data from over 250,000 mobile phone users and found use of mobile phones was not associated with risk of developing brain tumours.

However, there are some concerns about whether prolonged exposure could have other biological effects.

Some research has suggested possible links between mobile phone use and changes in testosterone levels, sperm motility and cardiac activity.

These findings have fuelled concerns, particularly around carrying phones close to the reproductive organs or heart.

But the evidence is far from conclusive.

Most studies examining electromagnetic radiation and its effects on human organs, including the heart, have found little evidence of a direct relationship.

However, one major UK longitudinal study found an association between longer weekly mobile phone use and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

The research found that sleep patterns, psychological distress and neuroticism accounted for between 2.25 and 11.5 per cent of the association.

Importantly, researchers suggested that the way people use their phones could be part of the problem.

READ MORE Facing fossil fuel criticism, Albanese urges world not to overlook Pacific climate plight

Late-night scrolling, disrupted sleep, constant notifications and the psychological stress of an endless stream of digital information can all affect the body's circadian rhythms, hormone regulation and metabolic health.

Poor sleep and chronic stress are already well-established risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

The researchers noted that these factors could help explain the relationship, although the study could not establish causation.

title: US resumes flights after air traffic problem sparks chaos
text:
In brief The ground stop was due to a communications issue affecting 22 regional air traffic control centres.

The US has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on.

The United States has lifted its order to ground all flights across the country after earlier communications problems at regional air traffic control centres.

The earlier notice from the Federal Aviation Administration said the ground stop was being imposed "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety".

Planes already in the air were allowed to land, but those on the ground could not take off.

The FAA made clear there was no connection between the problem and the Microsoft outage that disrupted millions of users on Friday. While many are now able to access their Outlook and Teams, the issue is still being fixed.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA was investigating a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports nationwide.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage."

"Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying," Mullin said.

Second ground stop since 9/11

Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes.

The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since US Congress approved US$12.5 billion ($18 billion) for the project last year.

Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fibre optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.

But Duffy said that another US$30 billion ($44 billion) will be needed to complete the work, which Congress has to approve.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the US northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.

"If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground," Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot, said.

"And not put them in the air where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them."

The US National Weather Service also said on Saturday it was experiencing nationwide internet and communications issues. There was no immediate indication the two incidents were connected.

title: 20,000 complaints a minute. How was the Microsoft outage fixed?
text:
Key Points Microsoft said services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications after the outage.

The disruption could result in over half a billion dollars in insurance claims, as billions more likely lost in productivity.

The Microsoft outage, which crippled popular services like Outlook and Teams, cost users over half a billion dollars, according to one expert.

Friday's outage lasted over 24 hours and prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars, and hosting virtual meetings.

Microsoft had over 450 million paid user licenses as of January 2026, according to its financial reporting, and over one billion devices connected to its services.

Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS told Reuters.

De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between US$300 million ($443 million) and US$500 million ($738 million).

Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.

Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.

READ MORE Microsoft says sorry for 24 hours-long global outage

Experts say the latest outage is a wake-up call for companies and users to have a backup plan for when services go offline.

How to prepare for future outages

RMIT Associate Professor of engineering Mark Gregory said companies in Australia have already been advised to plan for national telephone network outages after a series of failures.

"So if you're a Telstra customer, you need to have an Optus SIM card or something on another network as a backup," he told SBS News.

"If you're an Outlook or Microsoft user, you keep a Google or Gmail account as a backup so that you're still able to communicate or receive emails," Gregory said.

It's also important for companies, businesses, individuals and families to also have backups of software systems so that alternatives are available when one system fails, he adds.

He said businesses should also consider backups for human resource programs, billing, invoicing and accounting software.

"Unfortunately, I see many businesses that are not prepared to look at having that redundancy or backup approaches, and they simply rely upon everything being available," he said.

"And when it's not, their staff are really just being left in limbo."

Gregory said Australian businesses should have a mechanism to claim compensation, and the government should be able to fine big tech for outages that impact productivity.

"The loss of productivity will be in the tens of millions in Australia and tens of billions globally," he added.

What was the problem and how was it fixed?

Microsoft said the outage — one of the longest in Microsoft's history — was caused by server issues. The incident hit features tied to Exchange Online — mainly its cloud-based email and scheduling hub.

The company said a core process on the affected servers had become "overwhelmed". Once that happened, automated health checks within the system started shutting them down, tech expert Val Quinn told 7News on Saturday.

While the solution to the outage was to turn on the servers again, it wasn't that simple, Quinn added.

By the time the Microsoft engineers were ready to flip the switch on again, there was a huge reservoir of emails and messages queued up. Loading them all on in one go could create more problems, so they had to carry out the switch-on in stages, Quinn said.

Doug Jacobson, Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Iowa State University, said in a report on The Conversation that the pent-up messages were akin to a major highway crash.

Once the staged switch-on happens, email traffic does not instantly return to normal speed. Processing those long queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time — typically hours to days.

Is the crisis over?

Microsoft said that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications, ending the global outage that crippled online communications across businesses and governments for over 24 hours.

Dr Mohammad Goudarzi, from Monash University's Faculty of Information Technology, said engineers had been working to contain the outage's impact and restore services.

"Normally, in large-scale and interconnected systems, like Microsoft cloud platforms in this case, detecting a disruption may be quick, but identifying its underlying cause can take considerably longer," he told SBS News.

"These disruptions can also continue after access returns. Organisations may need to clear backlogs, check unfinished work and catch up on delayed decisions. Restoring the technology is only one part of restoring normal operations."

With additional reporting from Reuters

In April 2023, Travis Auld was left shattered after being overlooked for the biggest job in Australian rules football. Now, after swapping the AFL for Formula 1 and spending three years running the Australian Grand Prix, Auld is preparing to leave the country for a mysterious international business role he refuses to identify. He also revealed ambitious plans for the Australian Grand Prix Corporation to expand beyond motor sport and pursue other major events. “I quickly moved on from the disappointment, I suppose, of not getting the [AFL] CEO role,” Auld said. “I felt like the one thing I could control is what I did next.” Auld spent almost 25 years in football, including senior roles at Essendon, Gold Coast and AFL headquarters, before emerging as a leading candidate to replace Gillon McLachlan in 2023. When Andrew Dillon won the race for the AFL’s top job, Auld faced a choice: remain in the industry he had known for most of his professional life or test himself elsewhere.

He chose the latter, taking charge of the Australian Grand Prix Corporation despite admitting he knew little about motor sport or the organisation he was joining. “When you spend most of your career in one sport … you do wonder the extent to which those skills are transferable,” he said. “I remember when I made a decision to leave the AFL industry, I wanted to test myself doing something different. “It’s always nice when you take a risk with a view in mind that this might lead to another opportunity, or you might just learn some new things, and that’s what it ends up being. “I don’t know if you’re ever glad that you missed out on a job,” he said. “I’m still incredibly grateful for the experience I had, and I wouldn’t change a thing.” His next move will take him overseas with his family, completing a career transformation from an AFL administrator to an executive working on the international stage. Lando Norris in action during the Australian Grand Prix in early March. It’s truly a global sport,” he said.

“The partners are different, the demographic’s very different, the pace of innovation is very different.” Auld will leave the grand prix corporation confident in its future, revealing plans for the organisation to expand its operations beyond Formula 1 and MotoGP. “There’s an exciting plan in place for this organisation to broaden its reach in terms of hosting other events, in and out of motor sport,” he said. “We’ve obviously just signed up Supercars, but I think there’s an opportunity to broaden that beyond motor sport.” He also delivered an emphatic defence of Melbourne’s right to host the Australian Formula 1 Grand Prix, dismissing suggestions the event could eventually be relocated to another Australian city.

Asked whether he could envisage the race leaving Melbourne in his lifetime, Auld replied: “No, I can’t. I can’t.” The Victorian government has secured the event until at least 2037, and Auld believed the city’s major-events culture, infrastructure and international reputation made it almost impossible to replace. “If we’ve got to host an event somewhere in Australia, it’s pretty hard to beat Melbourne,” he said. He also rejected criticism of the taxpayer investment required to stage the event, arguing the economic and tourism benefits comfortably justified the cost. Auld revealed the Saturday night of the 2026 staging of the grand prix had delivered Melbourne’s highest hotel occupancy on record, while the event continued to attract international visitors and showcase Victoria to a global audience.

Health Minister Mark Butler has challenged states and territories that have banned puberty blockers for children to comply with new national guidelines, which suggest gender-diverse teens should get access to the treatment. The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) released an interim recommendation on Monday after the federal government launched a landmark review into the medical treatment of transgender children and adolescents in January 2025. Labor moved swiftly to interrogate the prescription of gender transition drugs, including puberty blockers, for young people after Queensland banned them, following the United Kingdom after a health service commission found there was little scientific evidence to support the treatment. Health Minister Mark Butler. Alex Ellinghausen The NHMRC recommended puberty blockers, or suppressants that delay hormonal development, be permitted across Australia for children whose gender-identity and sex recorded at birth don’t match. Prescriptions would have to be made in consultation with clinicians and parents as children begin to show physical signs of puberty.

Advertisement

The guideline does not require a diagnosis of gender dysphoria, the psychological distress about a mismatch of gender identity, to get treatment. The review acknowledged the low-certainty evidence for puberty blockers, but said guidelines must be provided for best practice. It noted the treatments were reversible. The council’s recommendation puts the Liberal government in Queensland and the Northern Territory, where bans on puberty blockers are in place, at odds with national guidelines, though the recommendation is not enforceable. Butler said all state governments had a responsibility to ensure the highest-quality care for all Australians. “I’m very confident that those state governments running these services will consider this advice very closely and make sure that their services are aligning with it,” Butler told reporters in Canberra.

Advertisement

Related Article Gender Puberty blockers and treatments for trans youth under review “I know traditionally, state governments of both political persuasions have always paid high regard to the advice of the National Health and Medical Research Council.” Butler emphasised the “unimpeachable reputation” of the NHMRC, which has set medical guidelines for decades. But those calling for a ban say there is not enough evidence the treatment is safe. “I have the utmost respect for the National Health and Medical Research Council, and I think the role that it has long played in this country at arm’s length from the government of the day and the political process to provide the highest quality clinical advice to health practitioners and the community generally should always be respected,” Butler said. “That’s why I asked them to try and review the evidence, and issue some pre-eminent guidelines to guide this contested, evolving area that’s the subject of so much public commentary and involves some of our most vulnerable members of the community.”

Advertisement

Queensland’s health minister, Tim Nicholls, rejected the new guidelines, saying the state government had made a clear decision on the provision of treatment based on its own independent review. “Our position remains unchanged, and we will continue to prioritise the health, safety and wellbeing of young Queenslanders,” he said. The state’s LNP government announced a ban in January last year on all publicly funded hormone treatments, including puberty blockers, for children under 18. The ban sparked a legal brawl between the parent of a transgender teenager and the government, with Nicholls using his ministerial powers to reinstate the ban after a Supreme Court judge ruled in favour of the parent. A class action against the ban was also launched in June.

Advertisement

New Zealand’s High Court last month struck down the national ban on puberty blockers, ruling that it amounted to unjustified discrimination and had not been subject to sufficient consultation. Butler on Monday acknowledged the UK Cass review had sharpened public debate in Australia. But he said the UK context was different, and was influenced by “pretty questionable private prescribing practices” and a less multidisciplinary model of care to Australia. The nation’s largest gender clinic, in Melbourne, prescribed 64 young people puberty suppressants in eight years, with an average wait of 530 days, Butler said. The NHMRC advice on puberty blockers is an interim guideline ahead of its broader recommendations on gender-affirming care such as the prescription of hormones, expected in 2028.

Critical Resources has secured a land access agreement for its Mayview antimony-gold prospect in New South Wales, finally clearing the way for boots-on-the-ground exploration of historic workings that previously delivered stunning rock chip grades of up to 52.3 per cent antimony. With access now approved by the local landholder, the company can begin a low-impact exploration program of soil and rock chip sampling, along with detailed geological mapping over some 270 metres of known historic workings. Critical Resources’ Halls Peak project area, which contains the Mayview prospect, is just 2.7km from Larvotto Resources’ Hillgrove antimony-gold operations in New South Wales. Previous rock chip sampling from historic workings and waste dumps at Mayview returned a suite of impressive results, including the headline 52.3 per cent antimony hit. Other samples recorded up to 38.3 per cent antimony, while another sample delivered a solid combination of 15.35 per cent antimony and 2.71 grams per tonne (g/t) gold. Further encouraging results include one hit of 12.45 per cent antimony and 2.18g/t gold alongside a second rock chip that registered 11.2 per cent antimony and 1.13g/t gold.

Advertisement

‘Mayview has returned some of the highest antimony grades we have seen at Halls Peak.’ Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither The prospect forms part of Critical’s 132-square-kilometre Halls Peak project in the New England Fold Belt, which hosts an inferred resource of 840,000 tonnes grading 3.7 per cent zinc and 1.5 per cent lead. Significantly, Mayview lies just 2.7 kilometres from Larvotto Resources’ major Hillgrove antimony-gold project. Nearby Hillgrove is being developed as a significant new non-China source, with Larvotto forecasting annual production of 4900 tonnes of antimony and 40,500 ounces of gold over an initial eight-year mine life. The company says that regional development adds weight to the geological significance of Mayview, where historic antimony-gold workings could be part of the same mineral-rich system that hosts Hillgrove, potentially extending southeast into Critical’s ground. The on-ground work is designed to give Critical the data it needs to define and rank drill targets for a potential maiden campaign. Any drilling campaign would require a further access agreement. Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “Mayview has returned some of the highest antimony grades we have seen at Halls Peak, and securing land access means we can now start the work needed to understand what sits beneath those historic workings.” *

Advertisement

The Mayview program comes as antimony has gained strategic importance following China’s export restrictions and a tightening global supply picture. As early-stage work in NSW gets underway, it represents only one part of the company’s multi-pronged global strategy. Critical’s other critical metals asset is its Mavis Lake lithium project in Ontario, Canada, where it has already defined a significant inferred mineral resource of eight million tonnes grading a solid 1.07 per cent lithium oxide. It is also undertaking grassroots exploration at its nearby Vermillion Bay lithium project. Notably, the company has also recently made an aggressive push into South American gold, securing a significant 228-square-kilometre ground package in Suriname. The portfolio includes three projects, Gadu Manda, Gonini and Greenstars, all sitting in the highly prospective Guiana Shield. The geological province is considered the South American counterpart to West Africa’s phenomenally rich Birimian Shield, home to 500 million ounces of discovered gold. The sizzle in Critical’s Suriname play is the nearology. Its Gadu Manda project lies just 4km from Chinese giant Zijin Mining’s 11.6-million-ounce Rosebel mine, a monster operation that has produced more than six million ounces of gold. Adding to the intrigue, small-scale artisanal miners have already been working the northern part of the Gadu Manda permit area, with pits and trenches exposing quartz veining. This potentially gives the company a ready-made set of walk-up targets, with the old-timers having already done much of the legwork scoping out near-surface gold. The region has also seen a flurry of corporate activity of late, led by Zijin Mining’s US$360 million (A$532M) acquisition of the Rosebel mine in 2023. More recently, gold giant Gold Fields tipped C$77 million (A$80M) into explorer Founders Metals for a 19.9 per cent stake and private investment house La Mancha took significant positions in other Canadian-listed explorers active in Suriname.

The strategic importance of antimony cannot be overstated, with the metal now listed as a critical mineral by Australia, the United States and the European Union. China, which dominates global production, tightened the export screws in 2024, sending prices soaring and leaving international buyers scrambling for alternative supplies. With its saddlebags full of high-grade surface samples and a major mine firing up just down the road, Critical Resources now has the keys to a very interesting piece of ground. The results from its first modern, systematic exploration program will no doubt be keenly anticipated by punters as it looks to determine if those eye-watering surface grades are just the beginning of a potentially bigger antimony-gold story at Mayview. A self-described “birth keeper” advised an expectant mother to “go home and rest” after two doctors told her to urgently present to the emergency department, the NSW Coroner’s Court has heard. Sita Kali – also known as Mumma Sita – was involved in the care of two of the four babies who died following a “free-birth” or homebirth in the NSW Northern Rivers region between 2022 and 2024. ‘Birth keeper’ Sita Kali was involved in the free-births of two babies who died in the Northern Rivers region. These four deaths are being examined at an inquest which started at Lismore Local Court on Monday. The families of the four babies who died declined to be involved in the inquest. The small but growing number of free-births fall entirely outside the medical system. As opposed to a planned midwife-led homebirth, a free birth mother may be alone, with a partner or unaccredited support person such as a doula or birth keeper.

Advertisement

Kali is based in the Byron region. Kali described her role as “a birth keeper [who] provides advice which allows women to make informed decisions as to the best way to birth their children”, the court heard. She does not carry any medical equipment that could assist women in a medical emergency. The court heard about a woman who had a “very strong desire” to homebirth but was out of area for her local hospital’s homebirth program. The woman instead planned to free birth with Kali and a doula. While midwives had estimated the woman’s due date was July 28, 2022, based on the scientifically proven method of calculating a due date based on her last period, Kali estimated a due date weeks later, on August 14 or 15, based on the likely date of conception. The woman did not give birth until 43 weeks and one day gestation, and the court heard Kali “played a critical and crucial role into altering [the mother’s] understanding as to when her baby was due”.

Advertisement

On August 18, the mother was “getting a little worried about being late on the hospital calculation”, however given she was “only one week after the date that Sita calculated … I felt OK”, the court heard. She attended an ultrasound on August 19, which found the baby had a very compromised heart rate, prompting the radiologist to urgently call her GP who contacted the mother to express his concern. Both doctors explained to the mother that her pregnancy had become a medical emergency which required a heartbeat monitor and birth within four hours. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Inside freebirthing: Empowerment, distrust and a growing dogma The mother said she was afraid of being “forced into a caesarean” if she attended hospital, and called Kali for advice.

Advertisement

“I advised [the mother] to go home and rest, calm herself down and consider what she wanted to do,” Kali said in her police statement. “My advice was that I wasn’t medically trained.” The baby was delivered on August 20 just after 8am, with the father, Kali and the doula present. The baby’s skin was white, had the umbilical cord wrapped twice around his neck, was not breathing and had faeces on his face. There was difficulty establishing breathing for a few minutes, but breathing returned following massage. Loading The mother had a preference for a lotus birth, which involves allowing an umbilical cord to dry and detach naturally, usually three to ten days after birth. The umbilical cord was still attached when paramedics arrived 12 hours later.

Advertisement

Kali recorded that the baby displayed signs of laboured breathing, but told the mother that holding him close to her chest would help. The pair discussed going to hospital, but decided it was not needed. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘These are avoidable’: Dozens of babies dead or permanently injured after freebirths Kali left before the baby had latched to feed, and the court heard that the baby never latched. In the evening, the baby developed hiccups and stopped breathing about five minutes later. Paramedics arrived just before 11pm, where they found a limp and hypoxic baby with a heart rate of over 100.

Advertisement

A number of attempts were made to intubate, but the baby was pronounced dead just after midnight. The baby’s father told police that in the brief time he was with them, he gave them love, and that he does not know or care about the baby’s cause of death. Kali has launched an online fundraising campaign to assist with her legal fees and had raised $4500 of her $15,000 goal on Monday. “My journey began with my own first birth, on the side of a mountain more than 26 years ago,” Kali’s fundraising site read. “That experience profoundly shaped my understanding of birth as a natural, physiological, emotional and spiritual process, and awakened a lifelong calling to support wombyn [sic] in reclaiming trust in their bodies, their instincts and their right to make informed choices.”

Locksley Resources has given its Greater Tottenham copper-gold project in central New South Wales a serious shot in the arm, unveiling an updated mineral resource of 10 million tonnes (Mt) at 1.10 per cent copper and 0.32 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 110,000 tonnes of contained copper and 100,000 ounces of gold. Notably, the new estimate represents a whopping 56 per cent jump in copper grade and a hefty 37 per cent lift in contained copper compared to the previous 2022 resource. Gold also joined the party, delivering a 36 per cent increase in grade and an 18 per cent boost in contained ounces, reflecting revised geological models, higher cut-off grades and pit-constrained reporting. The historic Carolina mine at Locksley Resources’ Greater Tottenham project in central NSW’s Cobar-Girilambone district. The updated resource consolidates three deposits, Mt Royal, Carolina and the Iron Duke prospect, into a single cohesive estimate. The work also boosts a portion of the resource into the higher-confidence indicated category for the first time. The Carolina deposit stands out as the highest-grade component, with its open-pit resource delivering 2.4Mt at a solid 1.22 per cent copper and 0.38g/t gold. The company says the deposit remains open down-plunge and to the north, offering the potential for further resource upgrades. The combined Carolina and Mt Royal deposits now host a combined 8.9Mt at 1.09 per cent copper and 0.27g/t gold.

‘The updated mineral resource estimate demonstrates the economic potential of the project.’ Locksley Resources technical director Ian Stockton Meanwhile, Locksley says permitting with the NSW Mines Department for its recently optioned Iron Duke project is well advanced for an initial 5500-metre program, designed from 28 drill pads. The campaign will target a 150-metre gap south of the existing resource in addition to infill and extensional drilling. Iron Duke is the most gold-rich of the three deposits, hosting a freshly updated inferred resource weighing in at 1.1Mt at 1.11 per cent copper and a healthy 0.61g/t gold. At the same time, the company is preparing a bigger 10,000-metre drill program for its Carolina and Mount Royal-Orange Plains prospects within the main Tottenham exploration licence to test sparsely drilled areas and chase extensions to known high-grade mineralisation. Adding another layer of blue-sky potential is the newly granted “Tottenham West” exploration licence. The ground adds 139 square kilometres to the portfolio and, more importantly, locks up an interpreted 10km-long structural trend with no historical drilling. The big resource upgrade clocks a key milestone in Locksley’s strategy of district-scale consolidation, having assembled a commanding 1000-square-kilometre land package within the Cobar Basin and Lachlan Orogen, home to major operations such as Tritton, CSA and the giant Cadia Valley operations. The NSW State Government has also recognised the region as prime copper country, with its Critical Minerals Strategy identifying copper as one of its five priority metals needed to meet the massive demand from global electrification and the energy transition.

Locksley Resources technical director Ian Stockton said: “The updated MRE demonstrates the economic potential of the project and presents the most complete picture of the Greater Tottenham mineral resource base to date, while the higher copper grades provide a stronger foundation for future resource growth.” While the resource upgrade provides a solid foundation, the real prize could lie in the substantial exploration upside still lurking beneath the surface. Locksley has outlined a hefty conceptual target of between 26 million and 53 million tonnes, grading 0.95–1.16 per cent copper and 0.24–0.31g/t gold. If the numbers stack up under the drill bit, the conceptual target could potentially deliver an additional 250,000–610,000 tonnes of contained copper and 200,000–530,000 ounces of gold. The company says the target covers the potential strike and dip extensions of the known lodes at Mt Royal, Carolina and Iron Duke, suggesting the current resource could just be the tip of the iceberg. The prospects lie along more than 50km of mineral-rich terrain, much of which has barely felt the bite of a drill bit. Locksley recently pivoted its entire focus to the Greater Tottenham copper-gold project after shelving its US antimony assets, going all-in on a district that now hosts a big resource upgrade. With a bigger, higher-grade resource in the bag, a district-scale footprint in a proven mineral field and a massive exploration target to chase, Locksley has laid out a clear pathway for growth. Aureka Limited has officially completed a transformational $8.9 million acquisition that instantly elevates the company from a Victorian gold explorer to a fully fledged producer. The deal delivers ownership of the producing Fiddlers Creek underground gold-silver mine and the strategically valuable Wedderburn processing mill. Notably, the assets have generated positive monthly free cash flow since the June quarter, according to the unaudited accounts. Completed on November 13, the deal to purchase High Grade Holdings, owner of Fiddlers Creek and Wedderburn, comprised $2.5M cash and $6.4M in shares, backed by a $7.65M two-tranche capital raise. The fourth covers Fiddlers Creek resource and reserve estimates, mining licence approval and expanded mill tailings capacity. Wedderburn could rapidly become the jewel in Aureka’s crown. One of just six gold processing mills in Victoria licensed to treat third-party ore, the fully permitted plant is currently ticking over at just 20 per cent of its 42,000-tonne annual capacity, based on 80 per cent uptime, leaving plenty of room to ramp things up, including a potentially lucrative toll-treatment business.

The first spoke is operating. Fiddlers Creek, in Victoria’s historic Percydale goldfield near Avoca, restarted underground production in July 2025. With extra staff and working capital, management is ramping up both operations. At Fiddlers Creek, the drill bit is turning on a 400-metre diamond drilling campaign, the first from surface since May 2025, chasing extensions to known high-grade gold zones and looking to add fresh ounces beyond the existing mine plan. The work forms part of a minimum 1800m drilling commitment over three years. Fiddlers Creek operates under a prospecting licence, approved work plan and planning permit, with a mining licence application pending. Meanwhile, Aureka is eyeing further opportunities at Wedderburn, including making better use of its existing mining licence footprint, expanding tailings capacity and securing additional ore to feed the underutilised mill. Next cab off the rank could be Aureka’s Comstock gold-silver project near St Arnaud, 45km southwest of Wedderburn. The former mine, last worked in 1995, hosts a 56,000-ounce inferred gold resource and could become the mill’s next ore source, subject to further approvals and a decision to mine. Further southwest along Victoria’s Stawell gold corridor, the company’s flagship Irvine gold project lies 130km from Wedderburn and 16km south of the Stawell gold mine, which has produced more than 5 million ounces. The longer-term growth play packs a hefty 398,000-ounce inferred resource and a separate conceptual exploration target of between 316,000 and 665,000 ounces, offering considerable scope to grow its gold inventory through further exploration.

Experienced metallurgist Marcus Binks, a former Fosterville processing manager involved in establishing Wedderburn, is expected to join the board as a non-executive director after the November 30 annual general meeting. The timing for Aureka’s entry into production looks shrewd, coming against a backdrop of historically elevated bullion prices. The World Gold Council reported an average September-quarter gold price of US$4262 (A$6000) an ounce, providing a potentially lucrative environment for emerging producers. By acquiring an operating mine and a scarce, underutilised processing plant, Aureka has sidestepped the lengthy and costly process of building from scratch. With a strong gold price and a pipeline of projects to feed its new mill, the company has rapidly assembled the core components of a regional Victorian gold business. title: One router, one bug. How routine upgrades caused worldwide chaos

Analysis TechnologyNetwork outage One router, one bug. How routine upgrades caused worldwide chaos David Swan November 16, 2026 — 3:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Microsoft wanted more capacity. America’s aviation regulator wanted to swap ageing copper cables for fibre. Last week, both got chaos. Microsoft’s email and office software went dark for millions of people from shortly before 5am AEDT on Friday, after an upgrade meant to add capacity. A day later, US authorities grounded every departing flight in the country for five hours after a contractor installed a router at a remote site in Arkansas. Microsoft’s email and office software crashed after an upgrade meant to add capacity. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth The two failures were unrelated and Microsoft says it has no indication its services played any part in the grounding. The upgrades themselves were defensible: old systems commonly have to be replaced, and software has to be patched – that’s normal. What failed was containment: one fault in one place was allowed to course through an entire network.

Advertisement

Australians felt it within hours. ASIO and the federal police lost email and so did councils, courts and schools. Australia Post pulled its phone payment system, while suppliers couldn’t tell supermarket distribution centres what was on the way. In Germany, 15 hotel guests were reportedly hurt by chlorine gas after a pool safety system that sent its warnings by email went silent. A tech company like Microsoft understands the risk as well as anyone. “There are no low-risk deployments to production,” its guidance to engineers warns, meaning no change to a live system is ever truly safe. Its advice is to change things in small steps, roll them out slowly, and stop at the first wobble. Microsoft has apologised over the global outage. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson On Friday the company said the outage “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” after a later network change. Its preliminary notices say traffic moved around during that maintenance and exposed a hidden bug in the systems that connect people to their mailboxes. Requests banked up until the servers choked. Then the dominoes fell. Work from the broken servers spilled onto healthy ones, which buckled in turn. Even servers that engineers revived “can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic”, Microsoft warned. Turning it off and on again took the best part of two days.

Advertisement

The flight grounding was similar: it started with a single router in El Dorado, Arkansas. Contractor L3Harris was installing it as part of a job replacing old copper communication lines with fibre. According to the Federal Aviation Administration, a flood of connection attempts then scrambled radio and radar feeds to 17 of the 22 US centres that guide planes between airports. That’s more than three-quarters of the system, toppled from one small site. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the routers “got overloaded with data”. Investigators haven’t yet established whether faulty equipment or a slip during installation was to blame. Flight tracker FlightAware counted about 9800 delays and more than 4700 cancellations, and US-bound flights from Sydney were held on the ground. Flights were grounded across the US. CNN Dr Mohammad Goudarzi, who researches cloud computing at Monash University, said the chaos stemmed from misaligned priorities. “Investment in reliability needs to keep pace with investment in new features,” he said.

Advertisement

Related Article Network outage Microsoft’s global outage and fixes: What we know The immediate question now for Australian businesses is who pays. Microsoft customers may be able to claim service credits, the small refunds written into their contracts. Prins Ralston, chief executive of the Australian Computer Society, the technology profession’s peak body, said those credits “won’t make up for a lost morning of trade for a small business”. A litigation funder, Victoria Peak, is already inviting affected Australian businesses to register for a possible class action, though no case has been filed. Ralston said there was a clear difference between who coped and who didn’t. “ASIO and the AFP had workarounds. Most small businesses and many agencies don’t,” he said.

Microsoft has promised a full post-incident report. Every Australian board should read it with one question of its own: when the next upgrade goes wrong, what still works? The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
